introduction-beyond-the-single-vpc.core: Real organisations have dozens to hundreds of VPCs across accounts and regions, plus on-premises data centres and offices. Connecting them means choosing between peering meshes, hub-and-spoke routers (Transit Gateway, Azure vWAN), encrypted tunnels over the internet (IPsec, WireGuard), and private circuits (Direct Connect, ExpressRoute, Interconnect), while managing routing, IP overlap, encryption and cost.

first_principles.problem: A company with 60 VPCs and 3 data centres has an unmanageable web of peerings and VPNs.
truths: Private circuits cost money but are predictable.
derivation: Use **Direct Connect** for steady, high bandwidth.

analogy.title: Building an airport hub system
analogy.story: Instead of direct flights between every city pair, flights go via hubs, with private charter for the busiest routes.
analogy.breaks: Airports add layover time; hub routing adds little latency but per-GB fees.

example.title: Target architecture
flow: DCs via Direct Connect + backup VPN

check.q: Why is planning non-overlapping CIDRs essential before connecting networks?
check.a: Overlapping ranges can't be routed between each other without NAT, blocking direct connectivity.

the-transit-gateway-your-central-cloud-r.core: AWS Transit Gateway is a regional, managed router. VPCs, VPNs, Direct Connect gateways and other TGWs attach to it, and TGW route tables decide which attachments can reach which. That enables transitive routing, segmentation (prod and dev isolated, shared services reachable by both) and central inspection via a security VPC. You pay per attachment-hour and per GB processed.

first_principles.problem: Dev VPCs can reach prod databases through a shared peering mesh, violating segmentation policy.

analogy.title: A central post office with sorting rules
analogy.story: Every branch sends mail through it; sorting rules decide which branches can send to which.
analogy.breaks: Post offices are slow; TGW adds microseconds but costs per GB.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Dev reaches shared services, never prod.

check.q: What's the difference between association and propagation in TGW?
check.a: Association decides which route table an attachment uses for lookups; propagation installs that attachment's routes into a route table.

vpns-connecting-over-the-public-internet.core: Site-to-site VPNs build encrypted tunnels across the internet between a cloud gateway and an on-prem router. They're quick to set up, cheap and encrypted, but throughput per tunnel is limited (about 1.25 Gbps on AWS) and latency and jitter follow internet conditions. Use two tunnels for redundancy, BGP for dynamic failover, and ECMP across tunnels for more bandwidth.

first_principles.problem: A branch office needs private connectivity to AWS today, and a Direct Connect circuit takes weeks to provision.
truths: The internet is everywhere and cheap.
derivation: Use **ECMP** with TGW for more bandwidth.

analogy.title: An armoured car on public roads
analogy.story: Contents are safe, but travel time depends on traffic.
analogy.breaks: Armoured cars have fixed capacity; tunnels too (≈1.25 Gbps each).

check.q: Why use BGP rather than static routes on a site-to-site VPN?
check.a: BGP detects tunnel failure and shifts traffic automatically, and advertises route changes dynamically.

vpn-types-route-based-vs-policy-based.core: Policy-based VPNs encrypt traffic matching specific source and destination selectors, with one security association per subnet pair. They're simple for two fixed networks but scale poorly and can't run dynamic routing. Route-based VPNs create a virtual tunnel interface: anything routed into it is encrypted, you can run BGP over it, and selectors are usually 0.0.0.0/0. Cloud VPNs and most modern designs are route-based.

first_principles.problem: Adding a new subnet requires renegotiating every policy-based tunnel's selectors on both sides.
derivation: Watch for **multiple SA** issues with cloud gateways.

analogy.title: A guest list vs a dedicated corridor
analogy.story: Policy-based checks each person against a list; route-based says anyone sent down this corridor is escorted securely.
analogy.breaks: Guest lists are easy to read; selector mismatches cause silent failures.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: New subnets just need routes, not new selectors.

code.text:
ip link add vti0 type vti local 198.51.100.20 remote 203.0.113.5 key 42
ip addr add 169.254.10.2/30 dev vti0 && ip link set vti0 up
ip route add 10.20.0.0/16 dev vti0     # or learn via BGP over vti0

check.q: Why can't you easily run BGP over a policy-based VPN?
check.a: There's no tunnel interface to peer on; encryption is decided by selectors, not routing.

ipsec-vs-wireguard-old-reliable-vs-moder.core: IPsec (IKEv2 plus ESP) is the interoperable standard: every router, firewall and cloud supports it, with many negotiable cipher suites and modes. That flexibility makes it complex to configure and debug. WireGuard is a small, opinionated protocol with fixed modern cryptography (Curve25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305), public keys as identity and in-kernel speed, but less vendor and cloud-gateway support and no built-in dynamic key distribution or routing.

first_principles.problem: A team spends days debugging IKE phase-2 mismatches between two vendors' firewalls.
truths: Fixed cryptography is simpler and safer.

analogy.title: A universal diplomatic protocol vs a private handshake
analogy.story: Diplomatic protocol works with every country but needs long negotiation; a private handshake is fast but only with those who know it.
analogy.breaks: Diplomats can improvise; IPsec peers fail on any mismatch.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: WireGuard config is far shorter; IPsec needed for cloud gateways.

code.text:
# strongSwan (IPsec)
conn aws
  keyexchange=ikev2
  ike=aes256gcm16-prfsha384-ecp384!
  esp=aes256gcm16-ecp384!
  left=%defaultroute  right=203.0.113.5  leftsubnet=10.0.0.0/16  rightsubnet=10.20.0.0/16

# WireGuard
[Peer]
PublicKey = 4mF...=
Endpoint = 203.0.113.5:51820
AllowedIPs = 10.20.0.0/16

check.q: Why can't you connect WireGuard directly to an AWS Site-to-Site VPN?
check.a: AWS managed VPN gateways only speak IPsec/IKE; WireGuard needs a self-managed endpoint (e.g. an EC2 instance).

direct-connect-bypassing-the-internet.core: Direct Connect (AWS), ExpressRoute (Azure) and Cloud Interconnect (GCP) provide private physical circuits from your network to the cloud at colocation facilities. They give consistent latency, high bandwidth (1–100 Gbps), lower per-GB transfer prices and no internet exposure. They take weeks to provision, aren't encrypted by default, and need redundancy across devices and locations to avoid single points of failure.

first_principles.problem: Nightly 20 TB data syncs over VPN are slow, variable and expensive in internet egress.
truths: Per-GB pricing is lower on DX.
derivation: Order **DX at a colo** (or via partner).

analogy.title: A private toll-free road to the warehouse
analogy.story: No traffic jams and cheaper per trip, but it takes time to build and a single road can be closed.
analogy.breaks: Roads are visible; you need monitoring to see a DX link degrade.

check.q: Is traffic over Direct Connect encrypted by default?
check.a: No; you need MACsec (on supported dedicated connections) or IPsec over the DX link.

types-of-direct-connect-dedicated-vs-hos.core: A Dedicated Connection is a physical port (1, 10, 100 or 400 Gbps) owned by you at an AWS DX location, with a cross-connect from your rack; it supports MACsec and multiple VIFs. A Hosted Connection is a slice (50 Mbps–25 Gbps) of a partner's port, provisioned faster where you have no colo presence, usually with one VIF. Choose by bandwidth, presence and lead time.

first_principles.problem: A company without a colo presence needs 500 Mbps to AWS within two weeks.

analogy.title: Owning a dock vs renting a berth
analogy.story: Owning a dock gives full control and capacity; renting a berth from a marina is faster and smaller.
analogy.breaks: Berths can be upgraded easily; hosted bandwidth changes may need re-provisioning.

example.title: Decision
flow: Need 500 Mbps, no colo → hosted via partner
Need 2×10 Gbps, have colo rack → dedicated
Need encryption at L2 → dedicated with MACsec
Need many VIFs → dedicated or hosted VIFs

check.q: When is a hosted Direct Connect the better choice?
check.a: When you need modest bandwidth quickly and lack a presence at a DX colocation facility.

macsec-securing-the-physical-link.core: MACsec (IEEE 802.1AE) encrypts Ethernet frames hop-by-hop at layer 2, in hardware at line rate, between two directly connected devices, such as your router and the AWS DX router on a dedicated 10/100/400 Gbps connection. It protects against taps on the physical path without IPsec's throughput limits, but only covers that link, not end-to-end. Keys are managed with MKA using a pre-shared CAK/CKN.

first_principles.problem: Compliance requires encryption on the DX circuit, but IPsec over DX caps throughput far below 100 Gbps.
truths: Hardware L2 encryption runs at line rate.

analogy.title: A locked pipe between two buildings
analogy.story: Anything flowing through the pipe is protected, but once it enters a building it's no longer in the pipe.
analogy.breaks: Pipes are visible; MACsec misconfig drops the link entirely.

code.text:
key chain DX-MACSEC macsec
 key 1000
  cryptographic-algorithm aes-256-cmac
  key-string <CAK>
macsec-policy DX-POL
 cipher-suite GCM-AES-XPN-256
interface HundredGigE0/0/1
 macsec network-link
 mka policy DX-POL
 mka pre-shared-key key-chain DX-MACSEC

check.q: Why choose MACsec over IPsec on a 100 Gbps Direct Connect?
check.a: MACsec encrypts in hardware at line rate, while IPsec tunnels have much lower throughput limits.
